text: Good morning, everyone. Miller, thank you so much. We're so excited to be here today. I think I look back over the past couple years and anytime we would had one of you in the room for an event like this would have been a great victory. But to have this set of powerhouse lawmakers here today, we have Senator Rick Scott from Florida, Senator Bill Haggerty from Tennessee, and the chairman of the House Financial Services Committee, Congressman French Hill. So I think that this is really evidence that the United States is the place to be for crypto innovation when we get this caliber of policymaker here to interact with the audience that we have today. So just to open up and maybe I'll start with you, Senator Scott, and then we can go down the line. I would love to hear why you think at a high level it's important for Congress to engage on digital asset and blockchain policy.
speaker: A

text: Well, first off, it's great to be here. Thanks for the opportunity to be here. I want to congratulate my colleagues that are here. If you look at the Genius act, these two individuals are really the key to making it happen. They busted their butt to make sure that we got bipartisan support. In Senator Haggarty's case, I can tell you in the Senate, which takes 60 votes, if it hadn't been for his hard, hard work, it wouldn't have happened and probably will be the only bipartisan bill that will pass this year and next year. So, and then, so he's done a great job. And then Congressman Hill, I used to live in, live in Tennessee. It's a great state. But his hard work over there is doing the exact same thing to get these things done. It's not easy to get the legislation passed. So I'm not a big program. I'm not a big government person. I'm a business guy. I get fed up with government. And one thing we've got to do is we always have to take the opportunity to make sure that the executive branch doesn't just have the chance to go, oh, it goes this way when somebody gets elected and it goes this way when the next person gets elected. The only way that's going to happen is if we pass logical legislation that makes sure we have a we know something is legal and we know how to do it. We have all the safeguards in there to protect consumers. But we got to make sure what we're doing, what you are doing is legal and, and you can innovate and you don't have the risk that somebody's going to come in and say, oh, you can't keep doing that. So it's a really exciting time, Senator Haggerty.
speaker: B

text: And for me, it's about the freedom and liberty that are at the very core of American society. This is a way to perpetuate this. And what we saw happen over the past four years was exactly the opposite. Major constraints on any effort to move in a direction that would have helped liberate the creative and innovative aspects of our economy. With respect to stablecoins in particular, you think about this. Today we have a payment system that was designed in the 1970s and 80s. It's archaic. It takes days to clear. What we're talking about with the stablecoin legislation, with the Genius act is to put us into the 24th century with a new payment system that takes advantage of the blockchain technology. We should be seeing an ecosystem built here that actually creates an opportunity for innovation to occur right here in America. And this specific bill, actually not only one puts us onto a modern day payment system, but it also extends the dollar's dominance as the vehicle of choice to do transactions around the world. And frankly, it stimulates demand for U.S. treasuries at a time where I think that's going to be beneficial. This is also a first major step as we move into much broader market structure. And I'd like to turn to Chairman Hill because he certainly has the greatest perspective on that. He's been putting a lot of time and effort for years and the zip.
speaker: C

text: Well, Kristen, it's great to be with you and Rick Scott and Bill Haggerty and with the Solana foundation family today at Accelerate. Delighted to be here. It's such important to have your views and your help to us in achieving the public policy goals that we have. I'm interested in this space because I've always been interested in technological advance that disrupts in finance and beyond finance. And we're at that transformational point and we have been for the past few years and the three of us are trying to bring it to fruition. Back in 1996, there was a moment just like this and the Congress didn't mess it up. I know you're shocked, but we passed the Telecommunication act of 1996. Chris Cox, our former member from California, also a former SEC chairman, Chris led that and he said, you know, we shouldn't mess up Web one. We shouldn't do anything to destroy the innovation that will happen on the Internet. And because of that work, we got the cell phone that's in your pocket, we got data that's roaming across that cell phone and we got an open Internet for innovation. Now flash forward to our work. We're at that same transformational moment for an operating system that's based on a blockchain, that's decentralized, that has all those benefits in what we call Web3. So we're fired up to be here. All three of us were successful innovators, entrepreneurs, business people before we were in Congress. We know that disruption is good, and so we're glad to be here.
speaker: D

text: I want to go to Senator Haggerty next because I want to dive a little bit deeper on the Genius Act. Over the past, I guess, week and a half, we've been the Senate has been looking and doing procedural votes to lead up to the consideration of this bill and we'll see some more amendments after the recess. But can you talk a little bit about, you know, a what the Genius act does, but also why it's so unique and rare to have this on the floor of the Senate and what the outlook is for passage of this legislation?
speaker: A

text: Certainly it's been enormously challenging to get this to the floor of the US Senate. The first major piece of legislation to move through the United States Senate Banking Committee in eight years was this stablecoin legislation, the Genius Act. And it took almost four hours worth of battling back and forth myself largely versus Elizabeth Warren, the ranking member of that committee. She seems to completely dislike anything that's decentralized. I think in her view, only a centralized answer that's frankly susceptible to choke point 3.0 seems to be acceptable in her mind. But after close to four hours of debate and committee respectful debate and I was ably assisted by Chairman Tim Scott and Cynthia Lummis back and forth over the net, it came to a vote. And at that point Senator Warren was able to hold five of her Democrat colleagues with her and oppose us. But five other Democrats came with us and made this the most bipartisan product to come out of the Senate Banking Committee in a decade. As it came to the floor, there was a major battle again put in place. And I don't know what was said, but Senator Warren again was able to impress upon her Democrat conference that they should tank the bill. They did it, and thanks to Leader Thune, who had enough belief in me and our capacity to come back and get this back on board, it took us about 10 days to really mount the support of the industry and really reflect to the difficulty Democrat members of the Senate that this is an important bill, it's a bipartisan bill, and frankly we have bipartisan agreement on the policy. The question is, are we going to allow politics to permeate? And that's what happened on the first vote. But we brought it back. This time we have strong, solid bipartisan support. 66 votes. We needed 60 to get it across the finish line. 66 votes have put us into the position right now where we're considering a large number of amendments to the bill. We all want to see this bill as strong as we possibly can, but we also want to see it passed. And that's going to have to happen as soon as we get back in Senate. We're going to be off in state work period this coming week. But as soon as we get back, that's going to be the primary focus of our attention, is to bring the amendment process together and to get this across the finish line. So I'm looking forward to that. And again, it will create the first regulatory framework for this modern technology that we've ever had in America. If we don't do it, we're going to continue to see the seepage of innovation from America overseas. If we get this done, we're going to put America at the forefront, not just of our payment system that's a great benefit, but also at the forefront of innovation in this critical technology bill.
speaker: C

text: Could you also reiterate how important it was for the industry to get involved and call our Democrat colleagues to get that bill on board? Because if they had not done that, you wouldn't have gotten your votes.
speaker: B

text: That is a great point, Rick, because we wouldn't have had this second bite at the apple had it not been for people in the industry informing their Democrat senators and their friends that this is critically important. This isn't just a political opportunity to come and, you know, mash around in the headlines. We've got to get this done if we want to see America remain at the forefront of innovation. And so the calls and the support from the industry were absolutely critical in our ability to flip this back and put it into a bipartisan framework. So thank you for your help with that. Please continue to do it because it's going to take us another 10 days to get to a point that we can then send it to the House of Representatives.
speaker: C

text: Well, we're really encouraged by the progress, and I know we're not totally out of the woods yet in getting this across the finish line, but we're all working hard and rooting for you to get that over to the House. Maybe we'll head over to Chairman Hill next because your committee has considered stablecoin legislation as well and also have certain circulated draft around market structure. And I know you have a hearing coming up after the recess on, I think, June 4th, but please tell us about where that stands and sort of what the outlook is for both the stablecoin and the market structure legislation.
speaker: A

text: Well, first let me say thanks to my good friend of five decades, Bill Haggerty, for his tenacity and perseverance to craft the leadership in the Senate as they, Rick and Bill just pointed out how challenging it has been to have Banking Committee legislation move. So it's yeoman's work. They've done a marvelous job. They've had strong bipartisan support and it's demonstrated by the vote that they've achieved. We too, have had bipartisan support for about four years now in the House on crafting a path forward for digital assets, but we had no help from Joe Biden or Gary Gensler. I know everybody's personal favorite that stalled out the momentum we had, I'd say, between 2018 and, you know, 2020 and the pandemic. So we've worked cooperatively with Senate banking on the stablecoin idea. But there's another companion piece we think is important to the ecosystem, and that's called Market Structure Structure. We've worked on that with the House Ag Committee on a bipartisan basis. And in 2023, so two years ago, we passed that across the House floor with 71 Democratic votes. So we have a history of strong bipartisan support on market structure to complement the critical need for a payment stablecoin. And as Kristen said, On June 4th, we'll have a hearing in the Financial Services Committee in the House. There will be a companion hearing the same week in House Agriculture Committee. And we're taking comments now on a revised market structure framework bill that builds on the success of 2023, but is very different, I would say less clunky, more streamlined. And Cynthia Lummis, John Bozeman, both in the Senate, have been so helpful to the work we've done on this. Senator Gillibrand from here in New York. But that work the same week that my friends in the Senate will be hopefully very successful in the stablecoin work. We will be advancing market structure through those hearings, and I hope that we can have that progress through the committee soon.
speaker: D

text: Both of those, I think, would be absolutely major unlocks for the industry going forward. So thank you. I next want to turn to Senator Scott. I think we've talked a lot about the importance of U.S. competitiveness and having innovation here. But there are also national security issues. There are privacy issues. There are a lot of other topics that get broadened when we talk about crypto policy. And I know you've been very supportive of legislation that would prevent the US from having a central bank, digital currency. But can you talk a little bit about some of the, you know, these other issues that are related to crypto policy?
speaker: A

text: So whether we like it or not, there's countries that don't like our way of life. They don't like our freedom. They don't want us to have success. And I think what's. If you look at what's happening in the world, you've got Communist China over here, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and they're going to do whatever they can to impact your adversely, your way of life. So what we've got to do is on our side, we need to do everything we can to team up with the democracies around the world. And we've got to work to make sure that the bad actors can't have an adverse impact on us. China clearly wants to have a digital currency and control and set up the regulatory environment and control things. So we've got legislation that will prevent that. So the way I think about it is we're going to end up, I think, going into two sort of trading teams. The American team on one side and the Chinese team and the bad guys on the other. But all of the international regulatory agencies, China's going to try to destroy our opportunities to have success, and we're going to have to fight that every day.
speaker: B

text: I actually have another question for Representative Hill. You mentioned earlier it was difficult in prior Congresses to work with the White House. Things have obviously changed. And I know earlier this year you got on stage and, and did a press conference with your colleagues in the Senate and your counterparts on the House Agriculture Committee. And we had David Sacks from the White House come. And I've never seen anything like that where you see the White House, the House and the Senate come together and commit to getting this done. We're also very excited. We have Beau Hynes from the White House who's going to be on stage later this afternoon. Can you talk a little bit about the engagement that the White House has had and sort of how you're working with them to get these issues around across the finish line?
speaker: A

text: You bet. It's night and day, and I know Senator Scott and Hagerty will agree completely. So a switch has been turned on, which is we have a President of the United States and Donald Trump, that is pro innovation, pro American leadership. He knows we're the largest, most liquid successful capital market in the world and in world history. And it's perfectly logical that we should also lead that in favor financial technology, as we have in many other areas of technology, in health care, in financial services, and chip design and development. So with that effort, he's mustering the resources of the executive branch at the sec, the cftc, the White House staff, under the leadership of a superb advisory team. Not only do we have a good Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessant, who understands this, but David Sachs, the President's advisor on artificial intelligence and digital assets, is working with both the House and Senate in a hand in glove fashion. How can we support the legislative effort and how can we drive regulatory reform? And both are working well. Let me add one other point on Rick's comment about a central bank digital currency under the leadership in the House from two Tom Emmer, our Majority Whip, Warren Davidson from Ohio. We have consistently said we don't believe that we should have a government owned, government directed, surveilled consumer central bank digital currency. We shouldn't do it. We want the private sector to innovate on the blockchain, bring payment solutions, manifest that and lead with an American first point of view about technology development. We don't want the government to do that. So we have marked up Tom Emmer's bill banning the implementation of a central bank digital currency through our committee, and that too will come to the House floor. I want to echo and thank Senator Scott for his focus on this in the Senate.
speaker: D

text: I might just add one point to this in terms of the involvement of the current administration because it started well before this administration took office. I met in Mar a Lago with President Trump and bitcoin miners to talk about all aspects of the ecosystem. And I tell you, it was demonized so much in the prior four years. The previous administration, Bitcoin, Nashville. President Trump had a response. You were there. It was just, it was absolutely amazing. And, and we conducted a roundtable. I helped put together a group of CEOs from this industry with President Trump and the insightful nature of his questions. You know, you could just see the machinations going on. He gets this. He gets the fact that this is massively innovative. It needs to happen here in America. And he's put the full weight and force of the White House behind it with a great team, David Sachs, Boheinz, they've done a great job from the White House. And, and as Chairman Hill said, Scott Bessen has Certainly a great grasp of this. And with Paul Atkins coming into the sec, and you know, by way of disclosure, Paul was at Vanderbilt with Chairman Hill and myself. So we've all been friends for many, many years. But with Paul entering the sec, I think we have a wonderful door opening for us to really move this technology and this industry forward in America.
speaker: C

text: Well, and I wanted to actually ask about, about the sec, because I know from my perspective at the start of this year, I saw we sort of had two tasks ahead of us as an industry. One was to undo the damage of the past, and then the next was to put in the framework that allows us to be competitive for decades to come. And I think the SEC has a unique role to play in both of these. I mean, they were very quick to roll back the SAB121 accounting guidance. They stopped all of the litigation that was happening against the industry that didn't make any sense and dismissed that with prejudice. So they can't come back, which is fantastic. And the crypto task force is now putting out guidance. They're thinking through potentially doing a rulemaking. Do you have any thoughts on what the SEC can do that can be helpful that might make your jobs in Congress a little bit easier or maybe a little bit more narrow and not have to do it all in one big giant piece?
speaker: A

text: I'll start, but I'm sure, I'm sure that Rick and French will have something to add to this. One thing I'd like to do is just go back for a moment. You talked about undoing the damage from the past. And I think the messaging is clear coming from the White House, coming from the Senate and the House of Representatives. We're ready to move forward here. We're looking toward the future. There's some things that happened in the past that are so regrettable. We're right here in New York. It reminds me of what happened to Signature Bank. They shut that bank down in a choke point operation because they didn't like what they were doing in the crypto industry. They still have signet. They trapped it, they took it away. It's been taken off the market. They were trying to do everything they could on a regulatory. You know, these are non elected, faceless bureaucrats that were trying to destroy an industry. And frankly, it had a real impact right here in this market. That's over. And leadership at the SEC absolutely gets this. And the mindset of Paul and the other commissioners there are very much embracing the industry. I think that message is going to come through loud and clear. Dropping litigation. The tactics of Gary Gensler were frankly reprehensible. Using the regulatory framework, the enforcement network, to come back and put regulations on companies and arrears. That is over, my friends. That is over. Moving forward, we'll put a regulatory, we'll put a legislative framework in place, working together, and we're going to have a regulatory framework that supports it rather than destroys it.
speaker: C

text: But, but that's why, that's why you have to have laws. Otherwise we give these bureaucrats the opportunity to make, to constantly change back and forth whatever they believe in. And guess what? I mean, there's the government's pervasive and they'll go after you if they, you know, there's a bunch of ways. And so you've got to, you've, Bill said this earlier, you have to be politically active. You have to make sure the right people get elected and you have to, you have to be clear of what your needs are because, you know, there's a lot of people in government that they believe their way is the right way and they'll use every lever they can to go after you.
speaker: B

text: Rick Scott's 100% right. And this is why we did the press conference with David Sachs, to show the integrated approach under Tim Scott's leadership, John Bozeman's leadership, our leadership in the House, including GT Thompson, who's the chair of the Ag Committee. And we wanted David Sachs there because, yes, they can use exemptive relief, they can make things better. They can pull back dumb, ignorant ideas like staff Accounting Bulletin 121, correct the mistakes of the past, but it's not permanent if we want to. And the three of us do not support pendulum swinging executive orders. And it's not just an Article one power thing. It's just, it's an uncertainty creator. And Rick said it best. If we pass laws, we get permanent change. And that's what protects innovation. That's why we want permanent tax laws. We want permanent laws that direct economic agencies to minimally impact the private sector. Maximize.
speaker: D

text: You don't invest if you don't know what the rules are.
speaker: B

text: And this is how we create a more stable, long term, more certain future. So a payment stablecoin with the force of law, a market framework that directs the SEC or the CFTC or the bank supervisors. Here are the rules. Let people innovate. That's why President Trump's goal of having these bills passed before the August recess, I believe is realistic. It will take massive work by us, but it is realistic to achieve that. And we should do it in the meantime, Hester Peirce, Paul Atkins leading at the Commission to what are the tools we can do in the meantime? And the same with Scott Bessant at Treasury, Tyler Williams at Treasury, Luke Pat headed at treasury soon, fast, I hope you know, to do what they can in the executive branch. But permanent law is what we need.
speaker: D

You've been there from before the beginning on this. You think about the staff. Luke Pettit, who's on my staff right now, is headed to treasury to be assistant secretary there. Absolutely. Great job. David Sachs and Beau Hines at the White House, all of French's staff, the banking staff and the Senate have been terrific. We've got so many people that have been involved in the sleepless nights. But our country, if we want to lead the world, as these two gentlemen have just outlined, we need bipartisan certainty that we're going to let America lead the way in fintech and blockchain development. And I believe that's going to happen in 2025.
speaker: D
